interactions.label: Which investigation is the definitive method for confirming a multiple pregnancy

params.question: Which investigation is the definitive method for confirming a multiple pregnancy and determining chorionicity?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Beta-hCG levels are higher in multiple pregnancies but cannot determine the number of fetuses or chorionicity.

answers.text: Clinical examination of fundal height and fetal parts

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: An unexpectedly large uterus and multiple fetal parts raise suspicion, but clinical signs are unreliable for confirming diagnosis or determining chorionicity.
First-trimester USS confirms the number of fetuses and determines chorionicity with over 95% accuracy — the single most important prognostic factor in twin pregnancy management.
MSAFP may be elevated in multiple pregnancies but serves as a screening marker, not a diagnostic or chorionicity-determining investigation.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. While clinical signs and serum markers can suggest a multiple pregnancy, only first-trimester ultrasound can reliably confirm the diagnosis and determine chorionicity.
Correct. USS at 11–14 weeks is the cornerstone of twin pregnancy care because chorionicity drives every subsequent management decision.

interactions.label: On a first-trimester ultrasound, the inter-twin membrane meets the placenta at a

params.question: On a first-trimester ultrasound, the inter-twin membrane meets the placenta at a sharp right angle with no visible wedge of placental tissue at its base. What does this T-sign indicate?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Separate placentas produce the lambda (twin peak) sign, where villi from both placentas grow into the membrane base, creating a visible wedge — not a sharp right-angled junction.

answers.text: Monochorionic diamniotic twins sharing a single placenta

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: In MCDA twins, only amniotic membranes form the inter-twin septum, so it meets the single shared placenta at a clean right angle. This pregnancy needs fortnightly surveillance for twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome.

answers.text: Monochorionic monoamniotic twins with no dividing membrane

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Monoamniotic twins have no inter-twin membrane at all. The T-sign requires a visible membrane meeting the placental surface.

answers.text: A normal variant that has no bearing on pregnancy management

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: The T-sign has critical management implications — it identifies monochorionic placentation, which carries the risk of TTTS and requires a more intensive surveillance schedule than dichorionic twins.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. The T-sign indicates monochorionic diamniotic twins — only amniotic tissue forms the septum, meeting the shared placenta at a sharp right angle without the placental wedge seen in the lambda sign.
Correct. The T-sign identifies monochorionic diamniotic twins — shared placental circulation means these pregnancies require closer monitoring than dichorionic twins.

interactions.label: A woman is diagnosed with monochorionic diamniotic twins at her 12-week scan. Wh

params.question: A woman is diagnosed with monochorionic diamniotic twins at her 12-week scan. What growth scan frequency and planned delivery gestation should her obstetrician follow?

answers.text: Growth scans every 4 weeks from 20 weeks; planned delivery at 38 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This schedule is appropriate for dichorionic diamniotic twins, the lowest-risk category. MCDA twins share one placenta and face a real risk of TTTS developing within days — four-weekly scans are too infrequent to detect it early.

answers.text: Growth scans every 2 weeks from 16 weeks; planned delivery at 36–37 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: MCDA twins share a single placenta, placing them at risk for TTTS. Fortnightly scans from 16 weeks allow early detection of fluid discrepancies, and delivery at 36–37 weeks balances fetal maturity against the risks of placental ageing.

answers.text: Inpatient monitoring from 28 weeks; planned caesarean at 32–34 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This intensive protocol is reserved for monochorionic monoamniotic twins, where cord entanglement in a shared amniotic sac poses an acute, unpredictable danger requiring continuous inpatient surveillance.

answers.text: Growth scans every 6 weeks; planned delivery at 40 weeks

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No twin pregnancy is managed with this low a scan frequency or this late a delivery gestation. Even DCDA twins, the lowest-risk category, are planned for delivery at 38 weeks.

overallFeedback.feedback: Incorrect. MCDA twins require fortnightly growth scans from 16 weeks and planned delivery at 36–37 weeks, reflecting the heightened risk from shared placental circulation.
Correct. Monochorionic diamniotic twins need fortnightly scans from 16 weeks and delivery at 36–37 weeks — an intensity that directly reflects their shared-placenta risk.

interactions.label: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is a complication common to all twin pregnanci

params.question: Twin-to-twin transfusion syndrome is a complication common to all twin pregnancies and is the primary reason dichorionic twins also require fortnightly surveillance scans.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: TTTS is specific to monochorionic twins because it requires shared placental vessels for unequal inter-twin blood flow. Dichorionic twins have separate placentas and separate circulations, so they need only four-weekly growth scans — not the fortnightly protocol that monochorionic twins require.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Well done. TTTS only occurs in monochorionic twins who share a placenta with inter-twin vascular anastomoses. Dichorionic twins have completely separate circulations, so TTTS cannot occur — their surveillance is four-weekly, not fortnightly.
